goldenPoints: Erb palsy C5–C6 gives waiter's tip hand; Klumpke C8–T1 gives claw hand with Horner syndrome
Axillary nerve dies at the surgical neck, radial nerve in the spiral groove, ulnar nerve behind the medial epicondyle
Common peroneal nerve at the neck of the fibula is the classic cause of foot drop
Corneal reflex: afferent V1 (nasociliary), efferent VII
Corticospinal tract crosses at the pyramidal decussation in the lower medulla
Branchial cyst = persistent 2nd pharyngeal cleft, anterior to sternocleidomastoid
Ductus arteriosus is the derivative of the left 6th arch artery
Oesophageal constrictions lie at 15, 25 and 40 cm from the incisors
Diaphragm openings: vena cava T8, oesophagus T10, aorta T12
Membranous VSD is the most common congenital heart defect
intro: Anatomy carries 17 questions in every FMGE paper. The recent papers are image-heavy and clinical: a fracture site means name the nerve, a congenital swelling means name the embryological remnant, a gait means name the muscle. Revise these 12 topics with the trap lines and you cover what the stems actually ask.

subject: Anatomy
tagline: FMGE asks Anatomy as clinical vignettes and image spots — nerve injuries, embryology defects and vertebral levels dominate.

topics.askedAs: Erb vs Klumpke, fracture-site nerve matching
topics.oneLiner: Erb = C5–6 waiter's tip; Klumpke = C8–T1 claw hand plus Horner.
points: Roots C5–T1; Erb's point is where six nerves meet — upper trunk formation, suprascapular nerve, nerve to subclavius, divisions
Erb palsy: upper trunk C5–C6 lesion at birth or shoulder trauma — waiter's tip hand (arm adducted, medially rotated, forearm pronated)
Klumpke palsy: lower trunk C8–T1 — claw hand from intrinsic muscle paralysis; T1 involvement adds Horner syndrome
Axillary nerve injured in surgical neck fracture of humerus — deltoid paralysis, loss of abduction, sensory loss over regimental badge area
Radial nerve in spiral groove (mid-shaft humerus fracture) — wrist drop; triceps spared because its branches leave before the groove
Posterior interosseous nerve lesion — finger drop only, wrist extension preserved (ECRL spared), no sensory loss
Median nerve at carpal tunnel — thenar wasting, sensory loss over lateral 3½ fingers, positive Phalen and Tinel signs
Ulnar nerve behind medial epicondyle — claw hand, Froment sign; ulnar paradox: higher lesion gives LESS clawing
Long thoracic nerve (C5, 6, 7) injury — serratus anterior paralysis, medial winging of scapula on pushing against a wall
Crutch palsy is classically radial nerve compression in the axilla; tingling along medial arm and hand points instead to lower trunk or medial cord

head: Erb palsy
Klumpke palsy
rows: Horner syndrome if T1 sympathetic fibres involved

topics.title: Brachial Plexus & Upper Limb Nerve Injuries
topics.trap: Wrist drop with mid-shaft humerus fracture is radial nerve in the spiral groove — not posterior interosseous, which spares wrist extension.

topics.askedAs: Palmar space infection, snuffbox fracture, claw mechanics
topics.oneLiner: Snuffbox tenderness = scaphoid fracture; clawing = lost lumbricals and interossei.
points: Anatomical snuffbox: floor is scaphoid and trapezium, radial artery runs through it; tenderness here means scaphoid fracture until proven otherwise
Midpalmar and thenar spaces are separated by the midpalmar septum; a central palm stab wound with stiff middle and ring fingers suggests midpalmar space pus
Claw hand is produced by lumbrical and interossei paralysis — unopposed long extensors hyperextend the MCP joints while flexors flex the IP joints
Median nerve supplies LOAF muscles: lateral two lumbricals, opponens pollicis, abductor pollicis brevis, flexor pollicis brevis (superficial head)
High median nerve lesion gives hand of benediction when the patient tries to make a fist
Golfer's elbow (medial epicondylitis): pain at flexor-pronator origin, positive reverse Cozen test — the mirror image of tennis elbow
Sudden pop, swelling and Popeye deformity after lifting overhead = rupture of the long head of biceps tendon
Biceps brachii is the powerful supinator of the forearm besides flexing the elbow — supination is its signature action
topics.title: The Hand: Spaces, Snuffbox & Motor Pearls
topics.trap: In ulnar nerve injury the claw is worse with a LOW lesion (ulnar paradox) — an easy examiner reversal.

topics.askedAs: Foot drop nerve, Trendelenburg muscle, bursitis sites
topics.oneLiner: Foot drop = common peroneal at fibular neck; pelvic drop on single-leg stance = gluteus medius failure.
points: Common peroneal (fibular) nerve winds round the neck of the fibula — the classic site; lesion causes foot drop with loss of dorsiflexion and eversion
Sensory loss over the dorsum of the foot with impaired eversion also fits common peroneal nerve injury
Deep peroneal nerve lesion alone loses dorsiflexion but eversion (superficial peroneal) is preserved
Trendelenburg sign: paralysis of gluteus medius and minimus (superior gluteal nerve, L4, 5, S1) — standing on the weak side drops the opposite pelvis
Femoral nerve (L2, 3, 4) supplies quadriceps — loss of knee extension and knee jerk; saphenous branch gives medial leg sensation
Psoas major, the chief flexor of the hip, inserts on the lesser trochanter
Vastus medialis (oblique part) is the key muscle preventing lateral displacement of the patella during knee flexion
Housemaid's knee is prepatellar bursitis from repeated kneeling; clergyman's knee is infrapatellar bursitis
Posterior tibial artery pulse is palpated between the medial malleolus and the tendo calcaneus (Achilles tendon)
Sciatic nerve (L4–S3) — tibial division is injured more often in posterior hip dislocation than the peroneal division; peroneal division suffers more in lateral injuries
topics.title: Lower Limb: Nerves, Gait & Bursae
topics.trap: Dorsiflexion loss alone does not localise — check eversion and inversion: tibialis posterior (tibial nerve) inverts, so its sparing separates peroneal from sciatic lesions.

topics.oneLiner: Corneal reflex: V1 in, VII out. Inside the cavernous sinus sit only the carotid artery and nerve VI.
points: Corneal reflex: afferent limb is ophthalmic division of trigeminal (V1, via nasociliary nerve); efferent limb is facial nerve (VII)
Abducens nerve (VI) runs INSIDE the cavernous sinus beside the internal carotid artery — the nerve most medial and first affected in cavernous sinus thrombosis
Nerves in the lateral wall of cavernous sinus, top to bottom: III, IV, V1, V2
Abducens supplies lateral rectus — test it by asking the patient to look laterally (abduction)
Hypoglossal nerve lesion: tongue deviates TOWARDS the side of the lesion on protrusion (genioglossus of the healthy side pushes it across)
Spinal accessory nerve (XI) supplies sternocleidomastoid and trapezius — injury causes weak shoulder shrug and weak head turning to the opposite side
Facial nerve lesion at the parotid or stylomastoid region gives lower motor neuron palsy of the whole face — patient cannot close the eye on that side
Lingual nerve is at risk in third molar extraction — loss of general sensation over anterior two-thirds of tongue and floor of mouth
Trochlear nerve (IV) is the only cranial nerve emerging from the dorsal brainstem and has the longest intracranial course
Olfactory (I) is the shortest cranial nerve; vagus (X) has the longest overall course
topics.title: Cranial Nerves & the Cavernous Sinus
topics.trap: Tongue deviates towards the lesion in lower motor neuron XII palsy, but away from the lesion in an upper motor neuron lesion.

topics.askedAs: Aphasia type from vignette, hematoma artery, sinus drainage
topics.oneLiner: Fluent nonsense speech = Wernicke; broken effortful speech = Broca; pterion fracture bleeds from the middle meningeal artery.
points: Broca area (44, 45) in inferior frontal gyrus of dominant hemisphere — lesion gives non-fluent, effortful speech with preserved comprehension
Wernicke area (posterior superior temporal gyrus, 22) — lesion gives fluent but meaningless speech with poor comprehension (sensory aphasia)
Paracentral lobule carries motor and sensory cortex for the lower limb and bladder control — its lesion affects leg and sphincters, not the face
Bilateral amygdala damage produces Klüver–Bucy syndrome: hyperorality, hypersexuality, docility, loss of fear, visual agnosia
Middle meningeal artery enters through foramen spinosum; fracture at the pterion tears it and causes extradural (epidural) hematoma
Great cerebral vein of Galen drains into the straight sinus
Neostriatum = caudate nucleus plus putamen; lentiform nucleus = putamen plus globus pallidus
Frontal lobe lesion gives personality and behaviour change — disinhibition, apathy, loss of social judgement
Anterior cerebral artery supplies the medial frontal and parietal cortex including the leg area; middle cerebral artery supplies the lateral convexity and speech areas
Subdural hematoma comes from torn bridging veins and is crescent-shaped; extradural is lentiform and limited by sutures
topics.title: Brain: Functional Areas & Vascular Anatomy
topics.trap: Paracentral lobule questions are really leg-area questions — an ACA territory lesion causing leg weakness, not a cord lesion.

topics.askedAs: Decussation site, Brown-Séquard picture, dissociated loss
topics.oneLiner: Pain and temperature cross in the cord; position and vibration cross in the medulla; motor crosses at the pyramids.
points: Corticospinal tract fibres cross at the pyramidal decussation in the lower medulla — about 90% form the lateral corticospinal tract
Dorsal columns (fasciculus gracilis and cuneatus) carry fine touch, vibration and proprioception; they cross in the medulla as internal arcuate fibres
Spinothalamic tract carries pain and temperature and crosses in the anterior white commissure within 1–2 segments of entry
Brown-Séquard syndrome (hemisection): ipsilateral motor and dorsal column loss below the lesion, contralateral pain-temperature loss starting 1–2 segments below
Syringomyelia interrupts crossing pain-temperature fibres — cape-like dissociated sensory loss over shoulders and arms with spared touch
Tabes dorsalis damages dorsal columns — loss of proprioception, sensory ataxia, positive Romberg, lightning pains, Argyll Robertson pupil
Subacute combined degeneration (B12 deficiency) hits dorsal and lateral columns together — proprioception loss plus spasticity
Scissoring gait reflects spasticity of thigh adductors from bilateral corticospinal (upper motor neuron) involvement
Anterior cord syndrome (anterior spinal artery): motor and pain-temperature lost, dorsal column sensations preserved
topics.title: Spinal Cord: Tracts & Lesion Patterns
topics.trap: In Brown-Séquard the pain-temperature loss is on the OPPOSITE side and begins a segment or two below the lesion — the favourite wrong option says same side, same level.

topics.askedAs: Branchial cyst remnant, arch syndrome, arch artery fate
topics.oneLiner: Lateral neck cyst at the SCM border = 2nd cleft; ductus arteriosus = left 6th arch artery.
points: Branchial cyst sits anterior to sternocleidomastoid at the junction of its upper and middle thirds — persistence of the 2nd pharyngeal cleft (cervical sinus)
First arch syndrome (Treacher Collins): hypoplasia of mandible and zygomatic bones, malformed external ears, down-slanting palpebral fissures
Each arch has its own nerve: 1st–V (trigeminal), 2nd–VII, 3rd–IX, 4th and 6th–X (superior and recurrent laryngeal branches)
Ductus arteriosus derives from the LEFT 6th arch artery; the right 6th arch largely regresses
3rd arch artery forms the common carotid and first part of internal carotid; 4th forms part of the aortic arch (left) and right subclavian root
Failure of fusion of the medial nasal and maxillary prominences produces cleft lip; cleft palate follows failure of palatal shelf fusion
2nd arch cartilage (Reichert) forms stapes, styloid process, lesser horn and upper body of hyoid; 1st arch (Meckel) forms malleus and incus
Thyroglossal duct cyst is midline and moves up with tongue protrusion — unlike the lateral branchial cyst
The recurrent laryngeal nerve hooks under the 6th arch artery derivative: ductus arteriosus on the left, subclavian artery on the right
topics.title: Pharyngeal Arches, Clefts & Neck Embryology
topics.trap: Branchial cyst is lateral and does not move with tongue protrusion — that movement belongs to the midline thyroglossal cyst.

topics.askedAs: Twin type by split day, duct remnants, commonest CHD
topics.oneLiner: Split at 9–12 days = one placenta, one sac (mono-mono twins); meconium at umbilicus = vitellointestinal duct.
points: Zygote splitting decides chorionicity: days 0–3 dichorionic-diamniotic; days 4–8 monochorionic-diamniotic; days 9–12 monochorionic-monoamniotic; after day 13 conjoined twins
Persistent vitellointestinal (omphalomesenteric) duct presents as meconium or discharge from the umbilicus in a newborn
Meckel diverticulum follows the rule of 2s: 2 feet from ileocaecal junction, 2 inches long, 2% of people, often presents by 2 years
Membranous ventricular septal defect is the most common type of VSD and the most common congenital heart defect overall
Midgut herniates physiologically into the umbilical cord at week 6 and returns by week 10, rotating 270° anticlockwise around the superior mesenteric artery
Failure of neural tube closure: cranial end (day 25) gives anencephaly; caudal end (day 27) gives spina bifida
The diaphragm develops mainly from the septum transversum, which also explains its C3–C5 (phrenic) nerve supply
Urachal remnant (persistent allantois) leaks urine from the umbilicus — contrast with meconium, which means vitellointestinal duct
topics.title: General Embryology: Twins, Gut & Heart Defects
topics.trap: Examiners swap the two umbilical remnants: urine = urachus (allantois), meconium/faecal = vitellointestinal duct.

topics.oneLiner: 15–25–40 cm for the oesophagus; T8–T10–T12 for the diaphragm.
points: Oesophageal constrictions from the incisors: 15 cm at the start (cricopharyngeus, C6), 25 cm where the aortic arch and left bronchus cross, 40 cm at the diaphragmatic opening (T10)
Diaphragm openings: vena caval at T8, oesophageal at T10, aortic at T12 — remember 'voice of America': Vena 8, Oesophagus 10, Aorta 12
Thoracic duct begins at the cisterna chyli (L2), crosses from right to left at T5, and drains at the junction of left subclavian and internal jugular veins
Azygos vein arches over the root of the right lung to join the superior vena cava — a portosystemic collateral route in portal hypertension
Phrenic nerve (C3, 4, 5) runs on the anterior surface of scalenus anterior and supplies the diaphragm — C3, 4, 5 keep the diaphragm alive
The sternal angle (of Louis) marks the T4/T5 disc level, the carina, and the start and end of the aortic arch
Left recurrent laryngeal nerve hooks under the aortic arch — enlarged left atrium or aortic aneurysm can cause hoarseness (Ortner syndrome)
Bronchopulmonary segments: 10 on the right, 8–10 on the left; the right main bronchus is wider, shorter and more vertical, so aspirated objects enter it

head: Opening
Level
Main structures
rows: Inferior vena cava, right phrenic branches

topics.title: Thorax: Mediastinum, Oesophagus & Diaphragm
topics.trap: The 25 cm constriction is asked as 'structure at 25 cm from incisors' — the answer is the arch of aorta crossing, not the diaphragm.

topics.askedAs: Varices veins, most dependent pouch, hernia triangles
topics.oneLiner: Varices = left gastric meets azygos; most dependent female pouch = rectouterine pouch of Douglas.
points: Pouch of Douglas (rectouterine pouch) is the most dependent part of the peritoneal cavity in a sitting or standing female — pus and blood collect here
Oesophageal varices form where the left gastric vein (portal) meets the azygos system veins (systemic) — a portocaval anastomosis
Other portocaval sites: paraumbilical veins (caput medusae), superior–middle/inferior rectal veins, and retroperitoneal veins
Portal vein forms behind the neck of the pancreas at L2 by union of the splenic and superior mesenteric veins
Splenic artery runs in the lienorenal (splenorenal) ligament with the tail of the pancreas
Anatomical left hemihepatectomy removes segments II, III and IV — so the quadrate lobe (segment IV) goes with the left lobe, not the right
Liver has 8 Couinaud segments, each with its own portal pedicle; the Cantlie line runs from the gallbladder fossa to the IVC
Indirect inguinal hernia passes lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels through the deep ring; direct hernia bulges medial to them through Hesselbach triangle
Cardinal (transverse cervical/Mackenrodt) ligaments are the chief supports of the uterus; the ureter passes under the uterine artery — 'water under the bridge'
Pudendal nerve (S2, 3, 4) leaves via the greater sciatic foramen and re-enters through the lesser sciatic foramen to run in the pudendal (Alcock) canal
topics.title: Abdomen & Pelvis: Peritoneum, Portal System, Hernia & Supports
topics.trap: Quadrate lobe belongs functionally and segmentally to the LEFT lobe — hemihepatectomy questions exploit exactly this.

topics.askedAs: Narrowest larynx part, tonsil artery, MRND structures
topics.oneLiner: Adult narrowest = rima glottidis; tonsil bleeds from the facial artery; MRND spares SCM, IJV and nerve XI.
points: Narrowest part of the adult larynx is the rima glottidis (glottic opening); in children it is the subglottis at the cricoid ring
Internal laryngeal nerve (branch of superior laryngeal) gives sensation ABOVE the vocal cords; recurrent laryngeal nerve supplies sensation below them
External laryngeal nerve supplies cricothyroid — its injury flattens voice pitch; all other intrinsic laryngeal muscles are supplied by the recurrent laryngeal nerve
Palatine tonsil's main arterial supply is the tonsillar branch of the facial artery; its bed is formed by the superior constrictor muscle
The tonsil's fibrous capsule lies between the tonsil and the superior constrictor — the plane dissected in tonsillectomy
Modified radical neck dissection preserves three structures: sternocleidomastoid, internal jugular vein and spinal accessory nerve; the external jugular vein is NOT preserved
Common carotid artery bifurcates at the upper border of the thyroid cartilage (C4); its pulse is palpated against the carotid tubercle of C6 (Chassaignac)
Submandibular (digastric) triangle contains the submandibular gland; the carotid triangle contains the carotid bifurcation and hypoglossal nerve
Parotid swelling with earlobe pain and inability to close the eye points to facial nerve involvement within the parotid gland
Neck lymph node levels: I submental/submandibular, II upper jugular, III middle jugular, IV lower jugular, V posterior triangle, VI central compartment
topics.title: Head & Neck: Larynx, Tonsil, Glands & Triangles
topics.trap: Sensation above the cords is internal laryngeal nerve — a favourite swap with the recurrent laryngeal nerve, which is sensory below the cords.

topics.askedAs: Epithelium type, cartilage type, landmark levels
topics.oneLiner: Type II collagen = hyaline cartilage; elastic cartilage never calcifies; subcostal plane = L3.
points: Fallopian tube is lined by simple columnar ciliated epithelium; trachea by pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium with goblet cells
Oesophagus is lined by stratified squamous non-keratinised epithelium; urinary tract by transitional epithelium (urothelium)
Hyaline cartilage contains type II collagen and is the commonest cartilage; articular cartilage is hyaline
Elastic cartilage (epiglottis, pinna, Eustachian tube) does NOT calcify with age — the epiglottis is the laryngeal cartilage least prone to calcification
Fibrocartilage (type I collagen) forms intervertebral discs, pubic symphysis and menisci, and has no perichondrium
Pressure epiphysis transmits weight and forms joint surfaces (head of femur); traction epiphysis is non-articular, at tendon attachments (greater trochanter)
The joint between epiphysis and diaphysis in a growing long bone is a primary cartilaginous joint (synchondrosis)
Talus begins to ossify in the 6th month of intrauterine life; clavicle is the first bone to ossify and the most commonly fractured bone at birth
First primary tooth to erupt is the mandibular (lower) central incisor, at about 6 months
Vertebral levels: subcostal plane L3, transpyloric plane L1, supracristal (iliac crest) line L4, cricoid cartilage C6, transpyloric contents include pylorus, gallbladder fundus and renal hila
topics.title: Histology, Osteology & Vertebral Levels
topics.trap: Proximal radioulnar joint (pivot) produces pronation–supination — stems asking 'which structure facilitates pronation-supination' want the pivot joint, not the wrist.
